                                  13          Before the Court are two administrative motions:
                                  14          (1) Google LLC’s (“Google”) Administrative Motion to File Under Seal. ECF No. 254.
                                  15          (2) Point Financial, Inc.’s (“PFI”) Administrative Motion to Consider Whether PFI’s
                                  16              Response to Google’s Motion for Partial Summary Judgment and Supporting Exhibits
                                  17              Should be Sealed. ECF No. 256.
                                  18   For the reasons set forth below, the administrative motions are GRANTED to the extent Google
                                  19   seeks redactions.
                                  20     I.   LEGAL STANDARD
                                  21          “Historically, courts have recognized a ‘general right to inspect and copy public records
                                  22   and documents, including judicial records and documents.’” Kamakana v. City & Cnty. of
                                  23   Honolulu, 447 F.3d 1172, 1178 (9th Cir. 2006) (quoting Nixon v. Warner Commc’ns, Inc., 435
                                  24   U.S. 589, 597 & n.7 (1978)). Accordingly, when considering a sealing request, “a ‘strong
                                  25   presumption in favor of access’ is the starting point.” Id. (quoting Foltz v. State Farm Mut. Auto.
                                  26   Ins. Co., 331 F.3d 1122, 1135 (9th Cir. 2003)). Parties seeking to seal judicial records relating to
                                  27   motions that are “more than tangentially related to the underlying cause of action” bear the burden
                                  28   of overcoming the presumption with “compelling reasons” that outweigh the general history of
                                        Case 5:25-cv-04033-BLF            Document 261           Filed 05/20/26      Page 2 of 11




                                   1   access and the public policies favoring disclosure. Ctr. for Auto Safety v. Chrysler Grp., 809 F.3d

                                   2   1092, 1099–101 (9th Cir. 2016); Kamakana, 447 F.3d at 1178–80.

                                   3           In addition, in this district, all parties requesting sealing must comply with Civil Local

                                   4   Rule 79-5. That rule requires, inter alia, the moving party to provide “the reasons for keeping a

                                   5   document under seal, including an explanation of: (i) the legitimate private or public interests that

                                   6   warrant sealing; (ii) the injury that will result if sealing is denied; and (iii) why a less restrictive

                                   7   alternative to sealing is not sufficient.” Civil L.R. 79-5(c)(1). Civil Local Rule 79-5 requires the

                                   8   moving party to provide “evidentiary support from declarations where necessary.” Civil L.R. 79-

                                   9   5(c)(2). And the proposed order must be “narrowly tailored to seal only the sealable material.”

                                  10   Civil L.R. 79-5(c)(3).

                                  11           Further, when a party seeks to seal a document because it has been designated as

                                  12   confidential by another party, the filing party must file an Administrative Motion to Consider
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   Whether Another Party’s Material Should be Sealed. Civil L.R. 79-5(f). In that case, the filing

                                  14   party need not satisfy the requirements of subsection (c)(1). Civil L.R. 79-5(f)(1). Instead, the

                                  15   party who designated the material as confidential must, within seven days of the motion’s filing,

                                  16   file a statement and/or declaration that meets the requirements of subsection (c)(1). Civil L.R. 79-

                                  17   5(f)(3). A designating party’s failure to file a statement or declaration may result in the unsealing

                                  18   of the provisionally sealed document without further notice to the designating party. Id. Any

                                  19   party can file a response to that declaration within four days. Civil L.R. 79-5(f)(4).

                                  20    II.    ECF NO. 254
                                  21           Google has filed an administrative motion to seal portions of its response in opposition to

                                  22   PFI’s motion for summary judgment and exhibits thereto. ECF No. 254. PFI has not submitted an

                                  23   opposition to Google’s administrative motion.

                                  24           Google separates its sealing request into three categories. The first category is “terms and

                                  25   phrases pertaining to Google’s confidential and proprietary technology at issue in this litigation.”

                                  26   Id. at 3. Google contends the disclosure of this information would reveal Google’s confidential

                                  27   technology and in turn “weaken the competitive advantage Google maintains in the marketplace.”

                                  28   Id. The second category consists of quotes or close restatements of provisions of Google’s
                                                                                            2
                                        Case 5:25-cv-04033-BLF          Document 261           Filed 05/20/26    Page 3 of 11




                                   1   confidential contracts with third parties pertaining to Google’s plans regarding the chip at issue in

                                   2   this litigation. Id. Google argues that the disclosure of this information would expose Google’s

                                   3   “strategic decision-making with respect to the terms offered to its contracting partners” and harm

                                   4   its competitive advantage. Id. The third category of information Google seeks to seal is non-

                                   5   public business information pertaining to Google’s agreements with third parties as to its plans for

                                   6   the at-issue chip. Id. According to Google, the public disclosure of this information would reveal

                                   7   Google’s strategy with respect to its contractual relationships and weaken its leverage. Id. at 2–3.

                                   8          As the sealing request relates to a response to a motion for summary judgment, which the

                                   9   Court finds is “more than tangentially related to the underlying cause[s] of action,” the Court will

                                  10   apply the “compelling reasons” standard. Ctr. for Auto Safety, 809 F.3d at 1099–101. The Court

                                  11   finds that compelling reasons exist to seal the materials Google identifies, because the “compelling

                                  12   reasons” standard is met for confidential business information that would harm a party’s
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   competitive standing if publicly disclosed. See Music Grp. Macao Com. Offshore Ltd. v. Foote,

                                  14   No. 14-cv-03078, 2015 WL 3993147, at *6 (N.D. Cal. June 30, 2015); Jam Cellars, Inc. v. Wine

                                  15   Grp. LLC, No. 19-cv-01878, 2020 WL 5576346, at *2 (N.D. Cal. Sept. 17, 2020) (finding

                                  16   compelling reasons for sealing “confidential business and proprietary information”); Fed. Trade

                                  17   Comm’n v. Qualcomm Inc., No. 17-cv-00220, 2019 WL 95922, at *3 (N.D. Cal. Jan. 3, 2019)

                                  18   (finding compelling reasons for sealing “information that, if published, may harm . . . competitive

                                  19   standing and divulges terms of confidential contracts, contract negotiations, or trade secrets”); In

                                  20   re Elec. Arts, Inc., 298 F. App’x 568, 569 (9th Cir. 2008) (finding sealable “business information

                                  21   that might harm a litigant’s competitive standing”).

                                  22          The Court also finds that the request is narrowly tailored. See Civil L.R. 79-5(c)(3). The

                                  23   Court’s ruling is summarized below:

                                   6   III.   ECF NO. 256
                                              PFI has filed an administrative motion to consider whether PFI’s response to Google’s
                                   7
                                       motion for partial summary judgment and supporting exhibits should be sealed. ECF No. 256.
                                   8
                                       Google submitted a statement in support of sealing. ECF No. 259. Although PFI maintains that
                                   9
                                       “none of these materials warrant sealing,” ECF No. 256 at 1, PFI does not oppose Google’s
                                  10
                                       request.
                                  11
                                              Google separates its sealing request into three categories. The first category is “terms,

recap_documents.plain_text:
Case 5:25-cv-04033-BLF       Document 252        Filed 05/06/26     Page 1 of 7




                                   1

                                   2

                                   3                                  UNITED STATES DISTRICT COURT

                                   4                              NORTHERN DISTRICT OF CALIFORNIA

                                   5                                         SAN JOSE DIVISION

                                   6

                                   7        GOOGLE LLC,                                    Case No. 25-cv-04033-BLF
                                   8                     Plaintiff,                        ORDER DENYING PLAINTIFF’S
                                                  v.                                       EMERGENCY MOTION TO
                                   9                                                       ENFORCE PRELIMINARY
                                            POINT FINANCIAL, INC.,                         INJUNCTION AND FOR
                                  10                                                       CONTEMPT SANCTIONS
                                                         Defendant.
                                  11                                                       [Re: ECF 141]
                                  12
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13            Before the Court is an “emergency” motion filed by Plaintiff Google LLC (“Google”),
                                  14   seeking to enforce the preliminary injunction issued by this Court and impose contempt sanctions
                                  15   against Defendant Point Financial, Inc. (“PFI”) for violating the preliminary injunction. See Pl.’s
                                  16   Emergency Mot., ECF 141 (redacted). The motion does not present grounds for emergency relief
                                  17   or, indeed, any relief at all. Accordingly, the motion is DENIED.
                                  18       I.   BACKGROUND1
                                  19            Google contracted with third party CNEX Labs, Inc. (“CNEX”) for the development of
                                  20   hardware and software (“the CNEX technology”) for use in the manufacture of certain computer
                                  21   chips compatible with Google’s infrastructure (“the Chips”). See Compl. ¶¶ 9, 17, ECF 1
                                  22   (redacted); Order Granting in Part and Denying in Part Google LLC’s Motion for a Preliminary
                                  23   Injunction (“PI Order”) at 2-3, ECF 109 (redacted). Google also contracted with third party
                                  24   vendors for the manufacture, testing, and assembly of the Chips using the CNEX technology. See
                                  25   Compl. ¶¶ 9, 17; PI Order at 2-3. Several years into the project, CNEX ceased operations and
                                  26   filed for bankruptcy. See Compl. ¶ 81 & n.6; PI Order at 3.
                                  27
                                       1
                                  28    A number of documents in this case have been filed under seal or in redacted form. The
                                       Background section is drawn from unsealed materials to avoid the necessity of sealing this order.
                                         Case 5:25-cv-04033-BLF          Document 252        Filed 05/06/26      Page 2 of 7




                                   1          In the wake of CNEX’s bankruptcy, Google continued working with its vendors to produce

                                   2   the Chips, taking the position that it has all necessary license and access rights to the CNEX

                                   3   technology under the Master Purchase Agreement (“MPA”) between Google and CNEX. See

                                   4   Compl. ¶ 89; PI Order at 3-4. PFI, a creditor of CNEX, asserted superior rights in the CNEX

                                   5   technology based on its security interest in CNEX’s assets resulting from CNEX’s default on a

                                   6   loan. See Compl. ¶¶ 87-88, PI Order at 4. PFI warned Google’s vendors that they should stop

                                   7   using the CNEX technology to manufacture the Chips for Google. See Compl. ¶¶ 90-91; PI Order

                                   8   at 4. PFI also indicated that it might sell the CNEX technology to recoup its investment. See

                                   9   Compl. ¶¶ 12, 97; PI Order at 4. Google asserted that PFI could not sell the CNEX technology

                                  10   because it contains Google’s trade secrets. See Compl. ¶¶ 12, 35; PI Order at 2-3.

                                  11          Google filed this suit against PFI in May 2025, asserting claims for: (1) tortious

                                  12   interference with contractual relationships; (2) violations of the federal Defend Trade Secrets Act
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   (“DTSA”), 18 U.S.C. § 1831 et seq.; and (3) violations of the California Uniform Trade Secrets

                                  14   Act (“CUTSA”), Cal. Civ. Code § 3426 et seq. See Compl. ¶¶ 110-158.

                                  15          The Court granted Google’s motion for a preliminary injunction based on its tortious

                                  16   interference claim and enjoined PFI “from taking any action intended to or having the effect of

                                  17   interfering with Google’s license and access rights” to the CNEX technology, including contacting

                                  18   any of Google’s vendors “for the purpose of taking any action intended to or having the effect of

                                  19   interfering with that relationship[.]” PI Order at 22-23. The Court denied Google’s motion for a

                                  20   preliminary injunction based on its trade secret claims, finding that Google had not identified trade

                                  21   secrets that would be disclosed through PFI’s potential sale of CNEX’s assets. See id. at 16-21.

                                  22          PFI began exploring ways to commercialize the CNEX technology in order to offset its

                                  23   loss on CNEX’s defaulted loan. PFI filed a motion in the Bankruptcy Court seeking to convert

                                  24   CNEX’s Chapter 7 case to a Chapter 11 case, and proposing a reorganization in which PFI would

                                  25   acquire a majority stake in CNEX and resume CNEX’s operations. See Birch Decl. Ex. A (Mot.

                                  26   to Convert), ECF 141-3. Google opposed PFI’s motion to convert and, the day before the

                                  27   Bankruptcy Court’s hearing on that motion, filed the present “emergency” motion in this Court to

                                  28   bar PFI from going forward with its reorganization plan. See Pl.’s Emergency Mot.
                                                                                        2
                                         Case 5:25-cv-04033-BLF          Document 252        Filed 05/06/26      Page 3 of 7




                                   1          This Court immediately issued an order noting that “Google appears to expect this Court to

                                   2   act within a matter of hours in order to block PFI from participating in proceedings that are

                                   3   scheduled before the Bankruptcy Court. Order Re Pl.’s Emergency Motion, ECF 143. This Court

                                   4   determined that “Google has not provided the Court with any factual or legal basis justifying such

                                   5   precipitous action,” and directed the parties to meet and confer regarding a briefing schedule and

                                   6   hearing date for Google’s motion. Id.

                                   7          While the parties were engaged in briefing the present motion, the Bankruptcy Court

                                   8   denied PFI’s motion to convert. See Def.’s Opp. Ex. 1 (Bankruptcy Court Order), ECF 150-1.

                                   9   Google nonetheless persisted in litigating the present motion. See Pl.’s Reply, ECF 155. Google

                                  10   asks the Court to find PFI in contempt of the preliminary injunction order and to impose monetary

                                  11   contempt sanctions against PFI that would be payable to Google. See id. PFI argues in its

                                  12   opposition and court-authorized surreply that it has not violated the preliminary injunction and has
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   no intention of doing so. See Def.’s Opp., ECF 150; Def.’s Surreply, ECF 116-1.

                                  14    II.   LEGAL STANDARD

                                  15          “A district court has continuing jurisdiction to enforce its injunction.” Hangarter v. Paul

                                  16   Revere Life Ins. Co., 289 F. Supp. 2d 1105, 1107 (N.D. Cal. 2003) (citing Crawford v. Honig, 37

                                  17   F.3d 485, 488 (9th Cir. 1994). “An injunction is enforced through the court’s civil contempt

                                  18   power.” Hangarter, 289 F. Supp. 2d at 1107.

                                  19          “Civil contempt in this context consists of a party’s disobedience to a specific and definite

                                  20   court order by failure to take all reasonable steps within the party’s power to comply.” Reno Air

                                  21   Racing Ass’n., Inc. v. McCord, 452 F.3d 1126, 1130 (9th Cir. 2006) (quotation marks and citation

                                  22   omitted). “Civil contempt is characterized by the court’s desire to compel obedience to a court

                                  23   order or to compensate the contemnor’s adversary for the injuries which result from the

                                  24   noncompliance.” United States v. Bright, 596 F.3d 683, 695-96 (9th Cir. 2010) (quotation marks

                                  25   and citation omitted). “The moving party has the burden of showing by clear and convincing

                                  26   evidence that the contemnors violated a specific and definite order of the court.” Stone v. City &

                                  27   Cnty. of San Francisco, 968 F.2d 850, 856 n.9 (9th Cir. 1992). “[A] finding of contempt must be

                                  28   accompanied by conditions by which contempt may be purged[.]” Bright, 596 F.3d at 696.
                                                                                        3
                                         Case 5:25-cv-04033-BLF          Document 252          Filed 05/06/26    Page 4 of 7




                                   1    III.   DISCUSSION

                                   2           Google asks the Court to issue an order:

                                   3           (1) enjoining PFI from taking any action in violation of the Preliminary Injunction
                                               through any entity owned and/or controlled by PFI, including but not limited to
                                   4           CNEX Labs, Inc.; (2) enjoining PFI from proceeding with its Chapter 11
                                               reorganization plan in violation of the Court’s Preliminary Injunction; and
                                   5           (3) holding PFI in contempt, warranting the imposition of contempt sanctions
                                               against PFI in an amount to reimburse Google for the costs and attorneys’ fees
                                   6           incurred by Google to oppose PFI’s Motion to Convert in the District Court and the
                                               Bankruptcy Court, and as further deemed just and appropriate by this Court.
                                   7

                                   8   Pl.’s Emergency Mot. at 10; Pl.’s Reply at 5, ECF 155. The Court addresses each item of

                                   9   requested relief in turn.

                                  10           A.      Motion to Enjoin PFI from Violating the Preliminary Injunction

                                  11           Google first asks the Court to issue an order “enjoining PFI from taking any action in

                                  12   violation of the Preliminary Injunction through any entity owned and/or controlled by PFI,
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   including but not limited to CNEX Labs, Inc.” Pl.’s Emergency Mot. at 10; Pl.’s Reply at 5.

                                  14   Google contends that PFI should not be allowed to “achieve through a resurrected CNEX what it

                                  15   cannot achieve itself.” Pl.’s Emergency Mot. at 1. At the hearing, Google argued that PFI’s

                                  16   recent acquisition of CNEX’s assets supports the need for the requested order, because PFI will try

                                  17   to commercialize the CNEX technology in violation of Google’s rights.

                                  18           PFI contends that Google is attempting to broaden the existing preliminary injunction to

                                  19   include new restrictions on PFI’s ability to commercialize the CNEX technology. See Def.’s

                                  20   Surreply at 2. PFI points out that the Court declined to include such restrictions in the preliminary

                                  21   injunction at issue. See id. Moreover, PFI contends that because it is in the earliest stages of

                                  22   determining how to commercialize the CNEX technology, it has not taken any steps that even

                                  23   arguably violate the preliminary injunction. See id.

                                  24           The Court finds that Google has not established a basis for issuance of an order enjoining

                                  25   PFI from violating the existing preliminary injunction. The preliminary injunction expressly

                                  26   applies to “PFI and any persons in active concert or participation with PFI[.]” PI Order at 22.

                                  27   That language would cover any violation of the preliminary injunction by PFI, whether acting

                                  28   alone or through a resurrected CNEX. The remedy for such violation would be civil contempt.
                                                                                          4
                                         Case 5:25-cv-04033-BLF          Document 252         Filed 05/06/26     Page 5 of 7




                                   1   See Hangarter, 289 F. Supp. 2d at 1107 (“An injunction is enforced through the court’s civil

                                   2   contempt power.”). Accordingly, the Court concludes that issuance of an order directing PFI to

                                   3   comply with a previous order is unnecessary and unwarranted.

                                   4          Whether PFI has violated the preliminary injunction through its efforts to acquire and

                                   5   commercialize CNEX’s assets is addressed in Section III.C, below, discussing Google’s request

                                   6   for imposition of contempt sanctions.

                                   7          Google’s motion to enjoin PFI from violating the preliminary injunction is DENIED.

                                   8          B.      Motion to Enjoin PFI from Proceeding with Ch. 11 Reorganization

                                   9          Google next asks the Court to enjoin PFI from proceeding with its Chapter 11

                                  10   reorganization plan. That request is moot in light of the Bankruptcy Court’s denial of PFI’s

                                  11   motion to convert.

                                  12          Google’s motion to enjoin PFI from proceeding with its Chapter 11 reorganization plan is
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   DENIED AS MOOT.

                                  14          C.      Motion for Contempt Sanctions against PFI

                                  15          Finally, Google asks the Court to hold PFI in contempt for violating the preliminary

                                  16   injunction. Google seeks an award of contempt sanctions to reimburse it for attorneys’ fees and

                                  17   costs it incurred in opposing PFI’s motion to convert in the Bankruptcy Court and briefing issues

                                  18   before this Court. PFI contends that it has not violated the preliminary injunction.

                                  19          Google has not come close to meeting its burden of showing by clear and convincing

                                  20   evidence that PFI violated a specific and definite order of this Court. See Stone, 968 F.2d at 856

                                  21   n.9. The preliminary injunction order enjoins PFI “from taking any action intended to or having

                                  22   the effect of interfering with Google’s license and access rights” to the CNEX technology,

                                  23   including contacting any of Google’s vendors “for the purpose of taking any action intended to or

                                  24   having the effect of interfering with that relationship[.]” PI Order at 22-23. Google argues that

                                  25   PFI’s motion to convert in the Bankruptcy Court was a bad faith attempt to interfere with

                                  26   Google’s license and access rights and/or Google’s relationships with its vendors. Google makes

                                  27   a similar argument with respect to PFI’s acquisition of CNEX’s assets. Google’s arguments are

                                  28   not well taken for the reasons discussed below.
                                                                                         5
                                         Case 5:25-cv-04033-BLF          Document 252         Filed 05/06/26      Page 6 of 7




                                   1           As an initial matter, Google has not cited any case in imposing contempt sanctions based

                                   2   on a party’s exercise of its right to file a motion in a federal court proceeding. A party generally

                                   3   may not be subjected to liability based on its exercise of the right to petition the courts. See Sosa

                                   4   v. DIRECTV, Inc., 437 F.3d 923, 934 (9th Cir. 2006) (“[T]o exercise its petitioning rights

                                   5   meaningfully, a party may not be subjected to liability for conduct intimately related to its

                                   6   petitioning activities.”).

                                   7           Google instead relies on its characterization of PFI’s motion to convert as being brought in

                                   8   bad faith. In support of that characterization, Google submits the transcript of the hearing on

                                   9   PFI’s motion to convert, in which the Bankruptcy Court opined that the motion was brought solely

                                  10   for the purpose of gaining leverage over Google. See Reply Ex. B (Bankr. Tr.) 10:19-11:14, ECF

                                  11   155-2. Even giving full deference to the Bankruptcy Court’s assessment of PFI’s motives, the

                                  12   filing of a motion to gain a litigation or settlement advantage does not equate to interference with
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   Google’s rights in violation of the preliminary injunction. Google cannot establish contempt

                                  14   based on a generalized assertion regarding PFI’s motives – the law requires that Google

                                  15   demonstrate PFI’s disobedience of a specific provision of the preliminary injunction order.

                                  16   Google has not done so here.

                                  17           Google’s request for contempt sanctions appears to be grounded in the assumption that

                                  18   PFI’s acquisition and commercialization of CNEX’s assets necessarily would violate the

                                  19   preliminary injunction. That assumption is not supported by the current record. The preliminary

                                  20   injunction does not bar PFI from attempting to recoup its investment by commercializing the

                                  21   CNEX technology. Google requested that such a bar be included to protect its asserted trade

                                  22   secrets, but the Court determined that “[a]lthough Google has identified trade secrets that it owns,

                                  23   it has not shown that PFI’s sale of the Customized Software and Tooling would likely disclose or

                                  24   otherwise misappropriate those trade secrets.” See PI Order at 20-21. Accordingly, at this time

                                  25   PFI is not restrained by the preliminary injunction from taking actions to commercialize the

                                  26   CNEX technology, so long as PFI does not otherwise violate the preliminary injunction. Google’s

                                  27   speculation that PFI will not be able to thread that needle does not establish a present violation of

                                  28   this Court’s preliminary injunction order.
                                                                                         6
                                         Case 5:25-cv-04033-BLF       Document 252         Filed 05/06/26   Page 7 of 7




                                   1          Google’s motion for contempt sanctions against PFI is DENIED.

                                   2    IV.   ORDER

                                   3          (1)    Google’s “emergency” motion is DENIED in its entirety; and

                                   4          (2)    This order terminates ECF 141.

                                   5

                                   6   Dated: May 6, 2026

                                   7                                                  ______________________________________
                                                                                      BETH LABSON FREEMAN
                                   8                                                  United States District Judge
